newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parliamentarian raps Bavaria on Scientology.
newsitem.headline: German parliamentarian raps Bavaria on Scientology.

text.p: The head of Germany's parliamentary interior affairs committee said on Friday he thought Bavaria was wrong to shut Church of Scientology members out of the civil service.
This was "not the right way" to go and it would be more efficient to conduct a tax audit of the organisation in Germany, Willfried Penner of the opposition Social Democrats told German Radio.
Penner said there could well be "members of this sect who have a firm conviction without being caught up in anything criminal or offensive".
Bavaria is the first of Germany's 16 regional states to impose restrictions on public sector employment of Scientology members.

The Church of Scientology, founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, gives would-be members personality tests and then offers courses and literature to help them realise what the organisation sees as their full potential.
The conservative southern state said on Tuesdsay it would require all state employees to fill out a questionnaire detailing ties to the Church of Scientology from November 1.

Applicants for state jobs, including teachers and police officers, would not be hired if they refused to fill out the questionnaire. Those already employed would face disciplinary measures if they declined, the state chancellery said.

The Church of Scientology said on Thursday it had filed a complaint with the United Nations against the German government for "flagrant violations" of the human rights of its members, prompted by Bavaria's decision.

Heber Jentzsch, president of the Church of Scientology International, accused Bavarian Interior Minister Guenther Beckstein of "reviving the German demon" and said Beckstein was was falling "back into the dark times of Germany's history".

"Beckstein, with totalitarian arrogance, is re-enacting the Jewish law of April 7, 1933, which forbade public sector employment of Jewish people," Jentzsch said in a statement released in the United States.
Famous members of the Church of Scientology include film stars John Travolta, Tom Cruise and his wife Nicole Kidman.
Leaders of Germany's regional states said last week they would consider whether the Church of Scientology should be put under surveillance by the government's anti-extremist watchdog.
The Church of Scientology says it has around 30,000 German members. The government puts the figure between 10,000 and 20,000.
